summary: Gives advice on writing an RTP payload format specification, with reading tips, design practices and a template.

eli5.summary: A how-to guide for writing the rules for putting audio or video into RTP packets.

questions: how to write an rtp payload format
what is an rtp payload format
subtitle: A practical guide for anyone defining how a codec's data is carried in RTP packets, with a template.

tldr.problem: A real-time data format cannot be sent over RTP until a payload format specification exists, and writing a good one needs knowledge of both RTP and the media format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives reading tips, explains the RTP header, signaling and transport details that matter, lists design features such as aggregation and fragmentation, describes the IETF process, and ends with a template.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational guidance that updates RFC 2736 and is itself updated by RFC 9751.

today: RFC 8088 is an Informational document that updates RFC 2736 and has itself been updated by RFC 9751; it has not been obsoleted. Its process descriptions reflect the state at publication in May 2017.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
An RTP payload format specifies how units of a specific encoded media are put into RTP packet payloads and how the RTP header fields are used. A real-time data format with no payload format specification cannot be carried over RTP (RFC 3550). Writing a good one is nontrivial.

RFC 8088 extends and updates RFC 2736, because experience has grown and new RTP profiles and robustness tools have appeared. It is a guide, not a specification, and the RFC says it uses no RFC 2119 language. It also covers where a format can be defined: the IETF, other standards bodies, or proprietary venues. The IETF, IANA and RFC Editor rules it describes are as they were at publication, and the formal rules take precedence.
sections.eli5: Before a video or song can travel in little packets, someone must decide exactly how to cut and label it. This book helps those people do it well.

sections.title: Preparing: What to Read and Which RTP Details Matter
sections.content:
The author first needs a solid understanding of the media coding specification. For example, video coded with inter-picture prediction will perform poorly if the designer ignores that prediction. The RFC then lists recommended reading: IETF process documents, RFC 2736 (which introduces Application Level Framing, so that each Application Data Unit is independently usable), the RTP specification and its profiles, and robustness tools such as redundant audio (RFC 2198), forward error correction and retransmission (RFC 4588).

Among the RTP header fields, two always need extra definition by the payload format: the timestamp and the marker bit. In audio the marker bit usually marks the start of a talk burst; in video, the last packet of a frame. The sequence number is often used to recover order, the payload type is bound dynamically per session, and header extensions must not contain information needed to decode the payload.

RTP has three multiplexing points: separate RTP sessions, separate streams by SSRC within a session, and the payload type field. Synchronization within a stream uses the timestamp; between media, SSRCs with the same CNAME in RTCP are matched and RTCP sender reports relate timestamps to a common NTP-format reference.
sections.eli5: Know your cargo and the postal rules first. Two labels on every box always need your own meaning: what moment the box belongs to, and whether it is the last box of a picture.

sections.title: Signaling, Media Types and Transport
sections.content:
Payload formats are identified out of band, usually by SDP (RFC 4566) with Offer/Answer (RFC 3264), RTSP or SAP. To avoid tying RTP to SDP, each format is identified by a media type, such as audio/PCMA, whose parameters are written as name=value. x- names are not suitable for documented formats.

Parameters need rules for each context. A declarative parameter, like a video level, is declared by one side for what it receives. A negotiated parameter must be accepted by the answerer or its payload type removed. Parameters about what an entity sends, such as the sprop- parameters of H.264 (RFC 6184), fit Offer/Answer poorly. Declarative use in RTSP and SAP can treat parameters differently, and the specification must spell out any difference.

On the transport side, the most common IP MTU at the time of writing is 1500 bytes, but links with smaller and larger MTUs exist, so designs must cope with both. The RFC also notes queuing behavior (tail-drop and bufferbloat, Active Queue Management) and Quality of Service markings as influences on RTP flows.
sections.eli5: Every payload format needs a name tag so programs can agree on it before talking. The tag can carry settings, and the rules must say who gets to choose each setting.

sections.title: Designing the Payload Format
sections.content:
The summary of design advice is KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid). The RFC warns against too many configurations, hard-to-implement formats, and special solutions that interact badly with general RTP tools. It then describes optional features, each to be considered for applicability rather than required:

  • Aggregation: several Application Data Units in one payload, which reduces header overhead but adds delay and reduces robustness against loss.
  • Fragmentation: splitting large units, which avoids IP fragmentation (often discarded by NATs or firewalls).
  • Interleaving and transmission rescheduling: spread burst loss over time, at the cost of delay and receiver buffering.
  • Media back channels: such as the codec mode request field in AMR, only for specific needs that generic RTP or RTCP mechanisms cannot meet.
  • Media scalability: temporal, spatial and quality layers, as in SVC (RFC 6190), transmitted as Single Session or Multi-Session.
  • High packet rates: the sequence number must not wrap within at least three RTCP reporting intervals; if it can, define an extended sequence number field.

The timestamp definition and clock rate are an active design choice. Video has commonly used 90 kHz, audio normally uses its sampling rate, and rates below 1000 Hz are not appropriate.
sections.eli5: Keep the packing rules simple. You may put several small items in one box, split a huge item over several boxes, or shuffle the order so one lost box hurts less. Each trick has a cost.

sections.title: Required Sections, Process and Tools
sections.content:
Every payload format document needs Security Considerations and IANA Considerations sections, and is strongly recommended to have a media format description and congestion control discussion. Security issues like confidentiality, integrity, replay protection and source authentication should normally be solved by mechanisms outside the payload format, with a reminder in the text. The format itself should call out risks such as decoding that is very costly for malicious input, active content, user data, and variable-bitrate audio that leaks information (RFC 6562). IANA registration covers the media type name and, where needed, new parameter registries.

In the IETF the work is done in the PAYLOAD Working Group, with steps from an individual draft through Working Group document, iteration and a Working Group Last Call of at least two weeks. Individual drafts are named draft-<lead author family name>-payload-rtp-<descriptive name>-<version>. Other standards bodies are urged to ask the Working Group for review, and proprietary formats should still be documented and registered, in the vendor tree under vnd.<vendor-name>. Section 8 recommends tools such as xml2rfc and the I-D Nits checker, and Appendix A is the template.
sections.eli5: A good rulebook must say how to stay safe and how to register its name, and there is a clear path to getting it approved. The book also comes with a fill-in-the-blanks form.
